summary: Defines terminology for benchmarking the control-plane performance of an SDN controller. It extends terms from RFC 7426 so that a controller can be benchmarked independently of the protocols and network it supports.

eli5.summary: Before racing cars, everyone must agree on words like lap and finish line. This agrees on the words for testing how fast a network controller works.

subtitle: Standard terms for measuring and comparing SDN controller performance independently of protocol details.

tldr.problem: Software-Defined Networking controllers have become critical infrastructure, but there is no standard way to measure and compare their performance, scalability, and reliability independently of the protocols they support.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extends the terminology from RFC 7426 with precise definitions for benchmarking terms such as topology discovery time, message processing rate, path provisioning performance, failover speed, and controller scalability limits.
tldr.outcome: Vendors and operators can benchmark SDN controllers using common terminology and measurement methods, enabling fair comparisons and informed purchasing decisions.

today: RFC 8455 is an Informational RFC that establishes terminology for SDN controller benchmarking. It is used alongside RFC 8456 (methodology) to measure and compare controller implementations independently of the northbound and southbound protocols they support.

sections.title: Role of the SDN Controller
sections.content:
Software-Defined Networking separates network control from forwarding. A centralized SDN Controller provides the control logic and programmability, exposing two interfaces: the northbound interface (where applications and orchestration systems tell the controller what to do) and the southbound interface (where the controller programs the actual network devices).

The controller maintains a Forwarding Table of flows learned either from traffic arriving at the data plane or statically provisioned through the northbound interface. It can operate in proactive mode (pre-programming flows before traffic arrives) or reactive mode (discovering flows from incoming traffic and computing forwarding rules on demand).

Controllers can run in standalone mode (a single controller managing all domains) or cluster/redundancy mode (multiple controllers in active/standby or active/active configuration for high availability). Benchmarking these varied configurations requires clear terminology, independent of the protocols used (OpenFlow, NETCONF, etc.).
sections.eli5: An SDN controller is like an air traffic controller at an airport: it tells all the planes (network devices) where to go based on what applications ask for. Different controllers work differently, so people need a fair way to test and compare them.

sections.title: Core SDN Terms and Configuration Parameters
sections.content:
The RFC defines essential SDN terms. A flow is a set of packets with matching source address, destination address, source port, and destination port (or any combination thereof). Asynchronous messages are control-plane messages generated by network devices to report events; the controller processes them and sends responses without blocking the device.

A path is a sequence of links through which traffic flows from source to destination. The RFC also defines Leaf-Spine topology, a common data center design where leaf switches connect to spine switches in a non-blocking fabric, useful for testing with realistic topologies.

Configuration parameters include the number of network devices under test, the number of cluster nodes if operating in redundancy mode, and test duration. Trial repetition allows results to be averaged over multiple runs to account for variability.
sections.eli5: Just like describing a car (engine size, color, weight), you need standard words to describe what an SDN controller does: how many devices it manages, how it handles requests from applications, and how it programs switches.

sections.title: Performance Metrics: Speed and Responsiveness
sections.content:
The RFC defines performance metrics for various controller operations. Network Topology Discovery Time is the time from when the first device connects until the controller has learned the complete topology. Asynchronous Message Processing Time is the delay from when the controller receives a message until it responds.

Reactive Path Provisioning Time measures the delay from when traffic arrives at a device (triggering a flow-miss) until the controller programs the new path and traffic begins flowing. Proactive Path Provisioning Time measures the delay from when the controller receives a request to pre-provision flows until those flows are active on devices.

The RFC also defines processing rates: Asynchronous Message Processing Rate (messages per second the controller can handle), Reactive Path Provisioning Rate (new paths per second in reactive mode), and Proactive Path Provisioning Rate (new paths per second when pre-provisioning). Network Topology Change Detection Time measures how quickly the controller notices and reacts when the topology changes (a link fails, a device goes down).
sections.eli5: These metrics measure how fast the controller works: how long it takes to discover the network, respond to requests, and program switches with new rules.

sections.title: Scalability: Size and Capacity Limits
sections.content:
Scalability measures the limits of what a controller can handle. Control Sessions Capacity is the maximum number of simultaneous control connections (e.g., OpenFlow sessions) the controller can support. Network Discovery Size is the maximum number of devices and links the controller can manage and represent in its topology database.

Forwarding Table Capacity is the maximum number of flow entries the controller can store in its internal forwarding table. This is important because large control planes (thousands of devices, millions of flows) require controllers that can scale efficiently. The RFC acknowledges that different controller implementations may hit different limits first—one might max out on session capacity, another on forwarding table entries.
sections.eli5: Just as you might ask "how many people can fit in an airplane," you need to know how many devices, flows, and connections an SDN controller can handle before it runs out of memory or processing power.

sections.title: Reliability: Failover and Recovery
sections.content:
Reliability metrics apply to clustered controllers. Controller Failover Time is the delay from when the active controller fails until the standby controller takes over and network devices reconnect to it. A short failover time means less disruption to traffic.

Network Re-provisioning Time is the time from failover until the new active controller has re-established the network topology and restored all flow rules. During this window, traffic may be dropped or delayed.

The RFC also defines Security aspects such as Exception Handling (how the controller handles malformed messages or protocol violations) and Handling Denial-of-Service Attacks (whether the controller can continue operating when receiving floods of malicious control-plane messages).
sections.eli5: If the main controller crashes, is there a backup? How long does it take for the backup to take over? How long until the network is working again? These reliability metrics measure how resilient the system is.
